The proposed method is a GPU-based hybrid method that combines the Modified Physical Optics (MPO) and Graphical-Electromagnetic Computing (GRECO) techniques.
The MPO component of the hybrid method modifies the surface normal vectors to improve the accuracy of the GRECO method in computing diffraction fields from wedges.
The GPU-based implementation of the hybrid method achieves significant speedups compared to a CPU-based implementation, with a maximum speedup of 41.43x for a model with 28,262 triangular facets.

The hybrid method was validated on several structures, including a 1m x 1m PEC plate, a 3m x 0.6m x 0.3m rectangular prism, and a simplified aerocraft model, showing good agreement with commercial software (FEKO) for both HH-polarized and VV-polarized monostatic RCS.

The GPU implementation uses CUDA parallel programming techniques, including assigning each visible triangle to a separate thread, storing triangle integral summations in shared memory, and applying a parallel reduction algorithm.

The hybrid method is particularly useful for computing electromagnetic scattering from electrically large and complex structures, which is important for applications in national defense, aerospace, and remote sensing.
The hybrid method was validated at frequencies ranging from 10 GHz to 350 GHz, demonstrating its applicability across a wide range of high-frequency electromagnetic scattering problems.
The hybrid method does not fully capture the creeping wave effects, which could lead to slight discrepancies compared to commercial software.
The main objective of the hybrid method is to obtain real-time results for the radar cross section (RCS) prediction of arbitrary target shapes using a graphics workstation.

The GRECO method was introduced in previous work for simple and fast computation of the Physical Optics (PO) surface integral, but it was complex to realize the wedges scattering, which is addressed by the MPO component in the hybrid method.

The GPU-based hybrid method uses a parallel computing approach, where each thread computes the scattered fields for a single triangle, and a parallel reduction algorithm is used to efficiently sum the contributions from all the triangles.
The hybrid method is validated by comparing the numerical results with those obtained through a serial computing program on a central processing unit, as well as through the FEKO method of moments.
The GPU-Hybrid and CPU-Hybrid results are nearly identical to each other, indicating that the GPU computation has no loss of accuracy compared to the CPU-based implementation.
The performance of the CUDA program is best when the thread size is increased, as this allows for more parallelism in the computation.

The speedup ratio of the GPU-based hybrid method compared to the CPU-based implementation increases as the number of triangular facets in the model increases, demonstrating the scalability of the GPU-based approach.
